passage: Sit, beta, and I'll tell you why I never followed the crowd. When I was fifteen, I'm Kiran in this story, I wanted Salma's table more than I wanted lunch. So I changed. I laughed at jokes I didn't find funny. I stopped bringing my sketchbook. I even copied the way they said "literally" every second word. For one month it felt like sunshine. Then Salma's group fell out over something small, and in the middle of it nobody could remember what I liked, because I had left nothing to remember. I sat alone with my tray, and the person I'd hidden was the only one I missed. A few weeks later I wandered into the art room, and a boy there said, "Oh, you're the one who draws bicycles!" I still have that sketchbook.

qa.q: What did Kiran stop bringing to school while trying to fit in with Salma's group?
What was Kiran feeling when sitting alone with the tray?
qa.a: Kiran felt a loss of self. The person Kiran had hidden was the only one Kiran missed, and nobody in the group knew what Kiran liked.

qa.q: What did Kiran learn about belonging that is worth passing on?
qa.a: Belonging bought by erasing yourself is fragile, so it is worth looking for people who like the real you, as Kiran found in the art room.

qa.q: How might Salma's group have seen Kiran during that month?
qa.a: They probably saw someone easy to agree with but hard to know, since Kiran had left nothing personal for them to remember.

grounding: Kiran badly wanted the popular table and reshaped everything about Kiran for it, then found that belonging built on self-erasure did not hold.
